content:
Senegal are African champions once again. More than ten months after a chaotic Africa Cup of Nations final in Rabat, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled on Tuesday that Senegal's 1-0 extra-time victory over Morocco stands, overturning the Confederation of African Football (CAF) decision that had stripped the Lions of Teranga of the title in March and handed it to the hosts.

The ruling, delivered unanimously by a three-person panel in Lausanne, ends one of the most extraordinary sagas in African football — though Morocco has already signalled that the legal fight may not be over.

"The Court of Arbitration for Sport has delivered justice to sport," Senegal's football federation said after the verdict, according to the Associated Press. For Senegal, it is a second Africa Cup title, following their first triumph in 2022, and a vindication of a team that had won the trophy on the pitch only to lose it in a boardroom two months later.

The final, played on 18 January in Rabat, descended into chaos late in normal time. With the score goalless and the match heading for extra time, hosts Morocco were awarded a controversial penalty in second-half stoppage time. Brahim Díaz stepped up — and missed. In protest at the award, most of Senegal's players walked off the pitch, and violent clashes broke out in the stands.

After an interruption of about a quarter of an hour, Congolese referee Jean-Jacques Ndala ordered play to resume. Both teams returned, the match was played to its conclusion, and Senegal won 1-0 after extra time to lift the trophy in front of a stunned Moroccan crowd.

That should have been the end of it. Instead, CAF's disciplinary process took over. On 28 January, CAF fined both federations over the incidents. Then, on 17 March, the CAF Appeal Board — acting on a referral from the Moroccan federation — ruled that Senegal had forfeited the final, recording a 3-0 default victory for Morocco and declaring the hosts African champions. The board based its decision on Articles 82 and 84 of the AFCON regulations, which cover teams refusing to play.

Senegal appealed to CAS on 25 March. A one-day hearing was held behind closed doors at the court's Lausanne headquarters on 8 October, before a panel chaired by French professor Gérald Simon, alongside German professor Ulrich Haas and Italian professor Luigi Fumagalli. The court had promised a verdict by the end of November, with a full written ruling setting out its reasons.

That ruling, issued on Tuesday, turned on a legal principle familiar to sports lawyers but rarely decisive in a case of this scale: the "field of play" doctrine. The panel held that the referee's decision to resume the match — or to stop it — fell "definitively within his sole authority", and that its effects were limited to the pitch. In resuming the game, the panel concluded, Ndala "did not err in law".

The reasoning matters because it draws a sharp line between what happens on the field and what a disciplinary body can revisit afterwards. As the court explained through its director general, Matthieu Reeb, the CAF regulations that would have meant forfeiture for Senegal "would have applied if the referee had blown the whistle to end the match definitively, which would have resulted in Senegal's defeat, but that was not the case". Ndala never ended the match. He stopped it, waited, and restarted it — and once both teams were back on the pitch and had expressed their willingness to continue, the result belonged to football, not to lawyers.

The panel also addressed the conditions in which Ndala made his call. It acknowledged the "extreme tension" and the challenging atmosphere in the stadium, but found that his decision to restart was not arbitrary and that his judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game. The decision was unanimous.

For Senegal, the verdict restores a title their players believed they had already won. Captain Sadio Mané, whose side had to be coaxed back onto the pitch in January, was among those celebrating the decision, with Senegalese media reporting scenes of joy in Dakar as news of the ruling spread.

Morocco's reaction was swift and defiant. The Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF) said in a statement that it intended to take "all the necessary legal steps" to challenge the CAS decision, and outlined plans for an appeal to Switzerland's Federal Supreme Court — the only body that can overturn a CAS award, and only on limited procedural grounds.

The Moroccan federation's challenge is expected to target one of the three judges on the CAS panel, raising questions about the integrity of a senior member of the tribunal. Reeb acknowledged that Morocco had submitted a protest just minutes before the verdict was announced, and the federation detailed its concerns in a statement protesting what it described as the court's failure to address potential integrity concerns. An appeal on those grounds would be unusual, but it is one of the few procedural routes available.

The saga has exposed deep tensions in African football governance. The Times, in its analysis of the ruling, described the reinstatement as a victory for football over politics, noting the widespread suspicion that the CAF Appeal Board's March decision to hand the title to the host nation had been politically influenced. The CAS ruling, by contrast, rested on a narrow and technical reading of who decides what happens during a match — and it sided with the referee.

What happens now is less clear. Senegal will expect the trophy, the medals and the record books to reflect what happened on the pitch in January. Morocco's appeal, if it proceeds, could take months, and CAS awards are rarely disturbed by the Swiss courts. But until any appeal is resolved, the celebrations in Dakar will carry a small caveat — and the most controversial final in Africa Cup history will keep one last chapter to write.

The full grounds of the CAS decision have been issued to the parties, and the court said the complete award will be published in due course unless the parties request confidentiality. summary: More than ten months after a chaotic final in Rabat, Senegal are African champions once again: the Court of Arbitration for Sport unanimously upheld Senegal's appeal on Tuesday, reinstating their 1-0 extra-time win over Morocco and setting aside the CAF decision that had stripped them of the title.
title: Senegal Regain Africa Cup Title as Sports Court Overturns Ruling That Handed Trophy to Morocco
